title: Revealing Hidden Unconventional Pairing through Nonreciprocal Transport
authors: Wen-Bo Dai, Ming Gong, Xianxin Wu, Chui-Zhen Chen, X. C. Xie
abstract: Identifying the pairing symmetry of Cooper pairs is a fundamental step toward understanding the microscopic mechanisms of unconventional superconductors. However, experimental identification remains a formidable challenge, particularly when unconventional pairing is obscured by a dominant $s$-wave component that masks its spectroscopic signatures. Here, we develop a symmetry-resolved framework to identify superconducting pairing symmetry through nonreciprocal conductance upon exchanging source and detector terminals in multiterminal devices. We show that nonreciprocal transport arises from symmetry-breaking components of the superconducting order parameter and exhibits a characteristic angular dependence that encodes the momentum-space structure of the pairing gap. In particular, time-reversal-breaking singlet pairing induces nonreciprocal charge transport, while spin-triplet pairing generates nonreciprocal spin responses, providing distinct transport fingerprints of the underlying order. We demonstrate this mechanism using representative models of iron-based and noncentrosymmetric superconductors and outline experimental protocols for multiterminal measurements. Our results advance the theoretical understanding of nonreciprocal transport in superconductors, and establish it as a symmetry-selective probe for identifying hidden unconventional pairing in a wide range of superconducting materials.
summary: The paper introduces nonreciprocal transport as a novel, symmetry-selective method to determine unconventional superconducting pairing symmetries. By measuring how conductance changes upon reversing current flow, researchers can isolate signatures arising only from symmetry-breaking components of the order parameter. This technique is highly valuable for characterizing complex materials where conventional measurements are ambiguous.
main_problem: The primary challenge is identifying the pairing symmetry of Cooper pairs in unconventional superconductors when the signal is obscured by a dominant s-wave component.
main_result: Nonreciprocal transport measurements provide a symmetry-resolved probe that can distinguish between different unconventional pairing symmetries (e.g., $s+id$ vs. spin-triplet) because pure s-wave states yield zero nonreciprocity.
method: The authors develop a framework using the difference in conductance ($\Delta G$) when source and detector terminals are exchanged in multi-terminal devices, which is sensitive to symmetry breaking components of the superconducting order parameter.
model_or_system: The study models superconductors (like iron-based or noncentrosymmetric materials) using an effective Hamiltonian incorporating both conventional s-wave pairing ($H_s$) and an unconventional component ($\lambda V_{un}$).
key_observables: Nonreciprocal charge conductance ($\Delta G_c$) and nonreciprocal spin conductance ($\Delta G_s$), which exhibit characteristic angular dependencies based on the underlying symmetry.
important_parameters: The magnitude of the unconventional pairing component ($\lambda$), the angle $\varphi$ (momentum space), and the ratio of disorder/roughness strength ($W/\mu$).
main_assumptions: The method relies solely on symmetry considerations, making it robust against a dominant s-wave background; calculations often use the Andreev approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how nonreciprocity arises from specific angular dependencies ($	ext{Im}[\psi_{un}(\varphi_k)]$ for $s+id$, or $d$-vector components for spin-triplet) and show comparisons between different pairing symmetries and external perturbations like interface roughness.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by defining nonreciprocity ($\Delta G$), demonstrates its sensitivity to symmetry breaking (comparing s-wave vs. unconventional), details how charge and spin channels probe distinct symmetries, and finally verifies the method's robustness against disorder and edge effects.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, experimentally accessible diagnostic tool for characterizing complex superconducting pairing states without needing direct spectroscopic measurements of the gap structure itself.
